note_tweet.text:
A great question from @TheStalwart. The answer is that of course we have lots of open questions in economics, but none of them will get answered by a theorem.  The question is not whether a statement is "true" but whether a model is useful to understand a given reality, and a model that may be useful to understand a reality may no longer be useful when the reality changes.

That does not mean that usefulness is determined by fashion. Take AI. A pure task-exposure model says radiology can be done by machines, hence radiology is replaced. In fact demand went up as shown by the fact that both wages and quantities of radiologists increased in the meantime(notice: useful model here, both P and Q go up, the mark of a demand shift). 

If not the tasks, what? With Jin Li and Yanhui Wu we argue that markets price jobs, not tasks, and that the impact of AI depends on whether the job is a "strong bundle" (tasks are hard to separate) in which case AI helps the workers, or "weak bundles" in which case it splits the job, and makes it narrower. If both types of jobs react the same to AI, our model is useless and must be discarded. 

Another example. Last year in Silicon Continent I argued for the "r without g" impact of AI potentially causing a fiscal crisis in europe (Rstar goes up everywhere due to higher expected earnings and investment boom, g only where AI is adopted, i.e. not in Europe) on the basis of the Auclert et al calibration of AS and AD for assets in their cool Jackson Hole (2025) paper. You can quantify the argument, figure out the elasticities, and the implied increase in rstar due to the AI revolution and test whether that accounts for the fiscal window narrowing. Again, is this model "true"?  Or just useful?

Neither theory nor empirics settle the question by themselves (as Leamer argued). Economists argue about it, and the data offers the empirical discipline of the argument. No model comes out as "the truth". The models that survive are the ones that are able to keep explaining what happens.

note_tweet.text:
Bill Gates offered his childhood friend Paul Allen $5 per share to buy him out of Microsoft. Allen refused and kept the stock that would eventually help make him worth an estimated $40B.

Months earlier, while Allen was undergoing cancer treatment, he had overheard Gates and Steve Ballmer discussing how to reduce his ownership in the company they had built together.

The 2 had known each other since school.

Allen was 15 when he met 13-year-old Gates. They spent their teenage years working with computers and eventually founded Microsoft in 1975.

But the ownership split had been a source of tension from the beginning.

Gates initially wanted 60% of the company.

Allen got 40%.

Later, Gates pushed for another adjustment.

64% for himself.

36% for Allen.

Allen agreed.

Microsoft kept growing. Its deal to supply software for IBM's personal computer put the business on a completely different trajectory.

Then, in 1982, Allen was diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma.

He began radiation treatment and gradually reduced his involvement in the company.

One evening in December, he walked past Gates' office.

Gates was talking with Steve Ballmer.

According to Allen, they were discussing his reduced productivity and how they could dilute his Microsoft equity by issuing stock options to themselves and others.

Allen stopped outside the door and listened.

Then he walked in.

He confronted both men and left.

That evening, Ballmer came to his house to apologize.

Days later, Gates sent a handwritten apology.

6 pages long.

But Allen had decided to leave.

In February 1983, he resigned from Microsoft.

Gates offered to buy his shares for $5 each.

Allen wanted at least $10.

Gates wouldn't pay it.

So Allen kept his stock.

When Microsoft went public in 1986, Allen still owned roughly 25% of the company.

As Microsoft grew into one of the world's largest businesses, his shares made him one of the richest people alive.

At one point, his fortune was estimated at $40B.

The 2 friends eventually repaired their relationship.

But Allen never forgot the conversation he overheard during his cancer treatment.

Gates had offered him $5 a share to leave.

Allen left.

His shares stayed.
